questions.question: Read the following passage cum cloze test and answer the following questions. In the wake of another abrupt rupture in Kathmandu’s ruling alliance, the latest crisis has laid bare the (1) ____ architecture of Nepal’s power‑sharing arrangements. A hastily brokered compromise unraveled when smaller partners balked at a timetable for rotating the premiership, triggering a (2) ____ of resignations and cross‑party defections that left parliamentary arithmetic volatile by the hour. Markets and ministries drifted as caretaker protocols (3) ____ major decisions, with infrastructure tenders and provincial budget releases stuck in procedural amber. Regulatory notices were issued and rescinded in quick succession, sowing uncertainty among investors and provincial administrators alike. Diplomats adopted a (4) ____ tone—affirming neutrality yet quietly flagging concerns about policy continuity, especially on debt management, hydropower concessions, and border coordination. For ordinary citizens, the spectacle felt (5) ____: familiar yet dispiriting, as if the rulebook were being rewritten mid‑game while everyday governance—price stability, service delivery, monsoon recovery—hung in the balance. What worried observers was not merely the fall itself, but the (6) ____ it created: hollowed‑out accountability, ad hoc rule‑making, and a steady erosion of trust that development can be insulated from politics. That conclusion may be premature; coalitions, by definition, trade durability for breadth. Yet unless parties converge on clearer rules of engagement—transparent rotation clauses, enforceable whips, and time‑bound agendas—the incentives to defect will continue to outpace the incentives to deliver. In the meantime, Nepal confronts a paradox: political competition is vigorous, but the state’s capacity to decide, implement, and reassure remains caught between calculation and drift. Select the most appropriate option for blank (1).

When embankments fail, soil liquefies; crops drown; grain spoils; and the year’s savings dissolve into sludge. Power lines snap; pumps fall silent; cold chains break; pharmacies run short as fevers rise. Schools turn into camps; certificates, land deeds, and exam papers curl into pulp; archives and photographs lose the faces that anchored families. Markets fracture when bridges collapse and warehouses flood, so prices lurch, fuel runs short, and small traders lose stock and credit. In panic’s wake comes the slower destruction: silted canals, poisoned wells, and microbes flourishing in warm ponds. Even the ground changes—riverbeds shift, gullies deepen, and footpaths vanish under braids of sand. People can rebuild walls and roofs, but a civilization is habit, trust, and continuity. When thousands migrate at once, neighborhoods scatter; elders are separated from care; apprenticeships and festivals skip a season; and gossip—the glue of daily order—goes quiet. Relief arrives, rescues succeed, and promises are made, yet the ledger of loss extends beyond money: it tallies time, belonging, and the confidence that tomorrow will resemble today. questions.solution:
The correct answer is Article 100.

Explanation:

Article 100(1) of the Indian Constitution addresses the voting procedure in Parliament, including the casting vote of the Chairman (in the Rajya Sabha) or the Speaker (in the Lok Sabha). According to this article, decisions in each House are made by a majority of votes from members present and voting.

Casting Vote: If there is a tie in votes, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is empowered to cast a vote to break the deadlock. This is known as the casting vote, and it ensures that the legislative process can move forward in case of an equal division of votes.
